text: Last lesson's formula recurring journal calculated one amount for one relationship. Allocations solve a related but bigger problem: spreading one pool of cost across many destinations at once, based on usage.

The core formula is simple: allocation amount per target equals the cost pool, times that target's usage factor, divided by total usage. Picture Solara Fixtures' facilities department with sixty thousand dollars in shared building costs for March, allocated across three cost centers by headcount. Manufacturing has eighty of the hundred twenty total employees, so it gets eighty over one twenty of the pool — forty thousand dollars. Sales gets fifteen thousand, admin gets five thousand.

One allocation definition, run once, generates the whole journal — a credit line relieving the facilities pool, and three debit lines spreading the cost by headcount. Nobody calculates three ratios and types three lines by hand every month.

That's why it's called mass allocation — a single rule can sweep across an entire range of targets, not just three cost centers but potentially dozens, using a parent-child hierarchy or a range of segment values. Add a new cost center to the business, and it just falls into the range the rule already covers.

Formula recurring journals and allocations both remove manual calculation, but allocations are purpose-built for one pool, many recipients, split proportionally by usage. Next up, lesson twenty: allocation rules and pools — the actual building blocks behind that definition.
